    Media Briefing: ChatGPT’s fresh business hub is an early ‘search console moment’ for publishers

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • Sources indicate that this Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m.
    • This week’s Media Briefing looks at what publishers can learn from ChatGPT’s fresh AI visibility and click data, how that data fits into their third-party analytics, and what it means for their GEO businesses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Sources indicate that this Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    This week’s Media Briefing looks at what publishers can learn from ChatGPT’s fresh AI visibility and click data, how that data fits into their third-party analytics, and what it means for their GEO businesses.

    OpenAI’s fresh Business Hub gives brands and publishers access to something they’ve never had before: a first-party view of how they appear in ChatGPT. But legal teams may need to read the fine print before publishers dive in.

    Last week, OpenAI launched a ChatGPT Business Hub, a dashboard for businesses that claim and verify their accounts. It offers data on how their sites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, website clicks and the topics driving discovery. For publishers, that offers an early view into activity they’ve largely had to estimate with third-party tools or infer from referral traffic.

    “Until now, everything publishers knew about their presence in ChatGPT came from third-party tools running prompts at scale and estimating, or from referral traffic after the fact. This is a very early, very limited Search Console moment for ChatGPT,” said John Shehata, CEO and founder of publisher SEO analytics firm NewzDash.

    In a recent development, publishing execs are mixed on how useful they thought the data would be for their AI visibility and audience development strategies. Of the half dozen large publishers Digiday spoke with for this story, half were in the process of setting up their business accounts.

    It’s early days, but one industry exec, who requested anonymity, mentioned legal teams may need to be extra cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms of service.

    OpenAI’s terms require businesses to agree not to pursue certain legal claims against the company, including disputes involving content published on their websites before they signed up. That may cause headaches for legal teams at publishers already grappling with how to protect and monetize their content in the AI era, if accessing valuable first-party visibility data comes at the cost of relinquishing certain legal rights — a trade-off that may give some pause before signing up.

    When reached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario.”.

    According to recent reports, despite those concerns, some publishers see a potential commercial benefit. Two publishing execs remarked they were interested in using the data to support their GEO offerings. AI attribution and measurement is a major hurdle for those businesses, but they said insights from brands’ first-party data could help publishers assess the performance of branded content campaigns alongside data from third-party tools.

    “These insights potentially provide a really valuable piece of the puzzle that should validate our own success criteria around visibility and citations,” mentioned Carly Steven, Daily Mail director of SEO and editorial ecommerce.

    Shehata said the Business Hub data could help publishers demonstrate the value of their GEO offerings to brands, but cautioned that a publisher’s own visibility metrics don’t prove a brand’s campaign delivered results.

    “With authorized access to a client’s data, [publishers can] finally prove that recommendations move real platform metrics. That closes the measurement loop missing from every GEO pitch. But a publisher’s own citation count is not proof of a client’s GEO return. A brand campaign still needs evidence at the brand level. The commercial opportunity is selling better evidence and better decisions, not citation counts,” he stated.

    Another publishing exec was less convinced the data would help their GEO business.

    “Since [the hub] is only [tracking] mentions of the business owner, it isn’t so useful to our needs around influencing AI answers on behalf of partner brands. But we are signing up just so we can see if there’s anything there,” the exec noted.

    In a recent development, for example, if a brand pays for a publisher’s GEO offering, that publisher produces sponsored content articles about that brand’s product, and ChatGPT recommends the product with a citation link to the publisher’s sponsored content, the Business Hub wouldn’t report the mention of the product to the publisher, the exec explained. This means publishers will need to continue to use third-party AI visibility tools to measure those citations.

    “At this stage, I see brand mentions in answers akin to billboards. It makes sense for Nike to have a billboard but not [a publisher],” the exec remarked.

    Lily Ray, vp of SEO strategy and research at performance marketing agency Amsive, pointed out that the Business Hub tracks mentions of a business website, rather than its brand name surfacing in ChatGPT.

    Industry observers note that that offers a “limited view” of what is considered a mention in ChatGPT, though Ray expects the measurement to evolve. It also makes click-through rates appear disproportionately high. On the Business Hub dashboard for her SEO consultancy, Ray recorded four clicks from just 25 mentions. While “they’re very small numbers in absolute terms,” Ray said the first-party data gives her another point of comparison against metrics from third-party tools.

    Sources indicate that while the dashboard offers an incomplete picture, Shehata said publishers can still use its data to establish a baseline and track changes over time. He recommends three steps  publishers take once they get access to their Business Hub data. The first is to use the data to set a baseline for mentions, clicks and discovery topics so that the publisher can evaluate trends over time.

    Industry observers note that the second is to use discovery topics, which are “the most valuable data for audience teams,” to steer editorial experiments, Shehata said. These topics show which themes ChatGPT associates with a publisher’s site, where the AI treats the publisher as an authority, and white spaces around topics the publisher wants to own.

    “A travel publisher seeing activity around family travel can strengthen those guides with original reporting and watch whether the numbers move,” Shehata noted.

    Publishers should also separate the metrics in the Business Hub dashboard and their outcomes, he added.

    “A citation is a visibility outcome. A visit is an audience outcome. A subscription or sale is a business outcome. Publishers need to measure those separately,” Shehata said. He suggested publishers compare Business Hub trends against their own analytics, such as ChatGPT referrals, newsletter signups and conversions.

    “If reported visibility grows while referrals stay flat, that raises a hard question about value the dashboard alone won’t answer,” Shehata said.

    The Business Hub analytics have a number of limitations that publishers should consider too,  Shehata noted. The data is aggregated, with no prompts, no per-article breakdown, and no competitor benchmarks, he said.

    Sources indicate that the lack of prompt data means the analytics lack what third-party prompt tracking can provide – and that’s saying something, considering prompt tracking is “deeply flawed,” remarked Barry Adams, founder of Polemic Digital, an SEO and audience growth consultancy for news publishers. Digiday previously covered the varying methodologies for gathering prompt data by different AI visibility analytics firms, and how much of it relies on synthetic data or panel data, and the efforts publishers have to go through to weed out the GEO solutions from the snake oil.

    “We don’t know the contexts in which our websites are mentioned, except in the vaguest of terms. That makes it very hard to glean anything useful from these reports,” Adams said. However, Adams pointed out that over time, Google added more useful tracking to its Search Console dashboard, and hoped the Business Hub would also continue to evolve.

    Even though the data is limited compared to what prompt tracking tools offer, the fact that the data is coming from the AI platform itself makes it “extremely valuable,” Ray stated.

    According to recent reports, “It’s another data point for a very convoluted channel,” she mentioned. “It’s not going to replace any of the tools I’m using.”.

    “This year, we kind of saw more volume. Smaller spends, but new advertisers. It’s too early to tell why that’s happening. If branded content is kind of going in a different direction because of AI and publishers are getting more media spend? I don’t really know. It’s been two wildly different years, this year versus last year.”.

    — John Sills, head of sales, North America at The Guardian.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Several advertisers in Spain, including consumer bank Santander, have paused their activity on TikTok due to concerns over videos containing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) circulating on the platform.
    • It has been revealed that the pause comes in response to reports from investigative journalism outlet Maldita.es published last week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Several advertisers in Spain, including consumer bank Santander, have paused their activity on TikTok due to concerns over videos containing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) circulating on the platform.

    It has been revealed that the pause comes in response to reports from investigative journalism outlet Maldita.es published last week. Two major advertising clients of another agency holding company have paused TikTok spending, Digiday understands, while energy company Moeve has also paused its TikTok activity according to reports in the Spanish press.

    The investigation found that videos that include CSAM, or promoted websites that sold CSAM, ran before or after ads from 21 brands including Ralph Lauren, Banco Santander, Pringles, Samsung, Philips, Nescafé, JD Sports and Apple.

    It has been revealed that in response to the investigation, Sira Rego, the Spanish youth and children minister, asked the country’s data protection agency to temporarily suspend access to the app. As of yesterday (November 16th), the matter is now being investigated by Spain’s public prosecution office.

    Santander, the fourth largest bank in Europe, suspended its advertising on TikTok following the investigation’s release. Publicis Groupe has held the advertiser’s global media and creative account since October 2025. Santander did not respond to a request for comment by time of publication.

    “We are aware and the team has been working with clients on the ground,” said an Omnicom spokesperson; they declined to say whether the holdco’s clients had also suspended TikTok activity.

    According to recent reports, spokespeople for Publicis Groupe, WPP, Havas and Dentsu declined to comment. Stagwell did not respond to a comment request by time of publication.

    TikTok has been attempting to reassure brands that its moderation systems can keep videos depicting abuse off its platform.

    According to a note circulated among advertisers and media agencies, the platform stated a “cross-functional task force” was responding to the Maldita.es reports. “We remain deeply committed to our platform being a safe and positive experience for teens,” said the note.

    Sources indicate that “Our automated moderation technology reviews content uploaded to TikTok to identify violations of our Community Guidelines. These systems examine a variety of signals, including keywords, images, captions, and audio. If a potential violation is identified, the automated moderation system will either forward it to our safety teams for further review or remove it automatically if it breaches our policies.”.

    So far, those measures have not reassured clients previously active on the platform. Laura Camazón, head of digital and innovation at Mediaplus Equmedia, stated three of the agency’s clients had paused their activity on TikTok.

    “Until we know what’s happening, it’s better to pause,” she told Digiday. Camazón said the agency’s clients will likely suspend paid activity on TikTok until 2027; she declined to name the  brands in question.

    In a statement provided to Digiday, a TikTok spokesperson mentioned: “We condemn child sexual abuse and exploitation. Child Sexual Abuse Material is categorically prohibited on our platform, and we deploy advanced detection technologies alongside a dedicated Child Safety Team to aggressively identify and eliminate it.

    Sources indicate that “Alongside these ongoing actions, as soon as these claims were published, we took further action to identify and remove content, and submit reports to The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children where appropriate. As bad actors continuously adapt their tactics, we work tirelessly to improve our safeguards, and we will continue to actively cooperate with authorities, as we have always done.”.

    According to recent reports, tikTok does not break out ad revenue data for Spain, but its combined advertising revenue for Europe, the U.K., Africa and Latin America totalled $9.2 billion last year. TikTok has around 26 million customers in Spain, according to EU filings.

    After 45 years of negotiating, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he plans to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Madison and Wall estimates creator marketing growing at double the pace of the rest of advertising, driven on by creator-led production investments.

    A newly introduced crop of companies promise to coordinate advertising budgets across platforms, but can they control buying decisions, or merely add another interface to the existing system?

    Own the end-to-end GTM Strategic Planning, covering territory design, segmentation design, target planning and GTM capacity planning.

    Translate firm priorities into field actions through designing the planning strategy and seeing it through to execution.

    Partner with Sales Leadership to design and iterate on coverage models, segmentation, and team structures that reflect how developers actually buy.

    Define and track the metrics that matter, and surface insights that drive action, not just reporting.

    Lead the Strategic Planning roadmap: guide and lead in tooling investments and evaluate upcoming systems and processes against real business needs.

    Work cross-functionally with talent acquisition, ensuring GTM and territory models stay aligned.

    Collaborate with GTM Engineering on automations and data pipelines so that your strategy translates into working systems, not just slide decks.

    Operate with high ownership. You set your own agenda, escalate when needed, and don't wait to be asked.

    Recent findings suggest that work asynchronously and document clearly. We're a globally distributed team and writing is how we think.

    It has been revealed that bridge strategy and execution. From drafting segmentation approaches in Google Docs to using SQL to monitor its effectiveness.

    Sources indicate that build for scale without over-engineering. Simple systems that work beat perfect systems that don't ship.

    Stay close to the customer. Developers are our buyers, and understanding how they discover, adopt, and expand is core to everything you'll do.

    Have 6+ years of experience in Revenue Operations, Strategy Consulting, GTM Strategy, or Sales Operations at a B2B SaaS or developer-tools company.

    Are fluent in the GTM stack: HubSpot, BigQuery, and Hightouch.

    Can write SQL comfortably and aren't afraid to get into the data yourself before asking an analyst.

    Have experience designing or overhauling sales processes, forecasting cadences, or territory models in a high-growth environment.

    Understand product-led growth motions: PLS, usage-based triggers, and how PLG data flows into commercial pipelines.

    Thrive with autonomy and are energized by building things that didn't exist before you joined.

    Communicate with clarity across Finance, Sales, Success, Partnerships, Engineering, and Marketing without losing nuance.

    In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    In a recent development, once a year, the entire company gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Industry observers note that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    It has been revealed that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #112512. GTA 6 could be a windfall for creators, but standing out will be tough

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1307 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    GTA 6 could be a windfall for creators, but standing out will be tough

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 spawned its own cottage industry in the creator economy.
    • Creators have spent months building toward the official launch today with hype videos teasing 24-hour marathons from top streamers like Kai Cenat and Darren Jason “IShowSpeed” Watkins Jr., and others dipping back into GTA 5 to capitalize on the buzz.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 spawned its own cottage industry in the creator economy.

    Creators have spent months building toward the official launch today with hype videos teasing 24-hour marathons from top streamers like Kai Cenat and Darren Jason “IShowSpeed” Watkins Jr., and others dipping back into GTA 5 to capitalize on the buzz. GTA 5 was the fourth most-watched video game on the platform in the last week, according to Twitch Tracker. Pre-launch GTA 6 views topped 40 billion views on YouTube, according to a spokesperson.

    The creator economy looks very different from when GTA 5 launched in 2013. This time, some creators have found ways to access GTA 6 early by switching regions, building anticipation before the official release. The day before launch, on November 18, it broke the all-time launch week streaming record with 7.88 million concurrent views, according to Steam Charts. Over the weekend, video game reviewers, streamers, musicians and athletes will play in the immersive game world and the real city it’s inspired by, Miami, Florida.

    “The scale of this is hard to even wrap our heads around,” stated Ashray Urs, head of Streamlabs, who said he hasn’t seen this level of interest in getting involved in streaming since the COVID pandemic.

    In a recent development, the immense popularity of GTA 6, which earned $1.5 billion in revenue before anyone could even play it, is both a boon and a hurdle for the creator economy. Streaming platforms will be inundated with live feeds. Standing out will be difficult, but crucial. Brand partnerships can pay dividends, but your content will need to meet expectations.

    Creators have been preparing for this moment for over a year, and two separate delays have only further complicated things. “Everyone has been thinking about this moment. Are you going to do a marathon? Are you going to do casual streams? Are you going to do video on demand [VOD] on YouTube?” remarked Reed Duchscher, CEO and founder of management organization Night Media. “A lot of our clients are just going to be constantly streaming.”.

    Cody “Clix” Conrad, a professional Fortnite player and streamer with 8.7 million followers on Twitch, is missing esports tournaments to make GTA 6 content, telling Digiday he and a group of his creator friends are renting a house to stream 24/7 (other streamer cohorts, including Vanoss Gaming, are doing something similar). The budget is “under 50k for the entire week” to create content, which he says is the “most efficient marketing spend of the week.”.

    Duchscher mentioned Night Media’s top streamers, which include Kai Cenat and Darryl Dwayne “DDG” Granberry Jr., aren’t just video game creators, and GTA isn’t necessarily their biggest event of the year (Cenat’s Streamer University pulls in millions of viewers and substantial brand partnerships). Still, he’s expecting they’ll have double their typical concurrent viewership. “We’re quite confident Kai’s going to have over 100,000 concurrents on his live stream,” Duchscher said.

    But Cenat has a built-in audience. For other creators, standing out may be tougher: Experts expect “tens of thousands of live streamers” to play GTA 6 in the coming days. Some think creators will have to “lean heavily” into short-form GTA 6 content to stand out.

    “There’s going to be a million moments that occur while you play the game over the weekend, [and creators will need to be] the most entertaining reaction of playthrough of those moments,” Conrad said.

    In a recent development, others should take advantage of the game’s ties to the real world. “The landmarks that were in Vice City [the fictional city in GTA 6], are probably the areas where you stream from,” Duchscher suggested. “You have to get really creative because the clippable moments are going to matter so much more.”.

    It has been revealed that another strategy for the coming weeks: Skip GTA 6 altogether. Nevada Carney, head of strategy at Mutiny, the gaming arm of social-first creative agency Saylor, said some of their partners are thinking about “counter programming.”.

    “Smaller creators who know it’s going to be so flooded with GTA might be more inclined to stream some other games that are two, three, or four on the list,” Carney said.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s a crowded creator field, but one that has been preparing for well over a year, planting partnership seeds that will blossom in the next few weeks. There have been some serious setbacks: Grand Theft Auto 6 was originally slated to release last fall, then delayed to this spring, then again to today. Those delays messed with brand budgets and partnership aims.

    “We thought this game was going to come out much earlier, and so we’ve had to move these back, which has then affected budget and has moved budget out of the fiscal year into another fiscal year, and we’ve had to then renegotiate,” Duchscher said.

    Conrad mentioned he doesn’t have any specific partnerships for his upcoming marathon, but hosted an IRL event in Miami themed around GTA 6 with his sponsor, JBL, the day before launch.

    Noah Eichen, executive creative director at Mutiny, noted the brands they work with have pushed planned partnerships and activations into late December or early next year to accommodate.

    Industry observers note that “There’s a lot of allocation of budgets that happens that way, just to kind build around this behemoth, knowing that it’s coming…it’s unavoidable. But I think that everyone’s been planning for it for so long that a lot of those budgets got shored up a long time ago,” Eichen mentioned.

    According to recent reports, interestingly, brand safety appears to be less of a concern than in the past, according to Mike Murphy O’Reilly, chief revenue officer at Dexerto. “GTA has always been one of those things for brands that, when you talk about advertising or doing something in gaming […] it’s at the top of that list as an absolute no,” he said. “GTA 6…the moment is significant enough they’re willing to break their brand safety rules.”.

    There’s also the expectation that GTA 6 will have a very long tail. The game is launching without its infamous multiplayer mode, which kept the previous installment alive and thriving for 13 years. That mode, known as GTA Online, spawned role-playing communities of content creators (known as GTA RP) that drew millions of eyes and sponsors.

    “Brands are trying to figure out the longevity of the partnerships…if they can’t get into GTA now, they know their brand can get into episodic type content that will be started with RP,” noted Carney. “Brands are scrambling at the moment because they don’t know how to use their media spend…that seems like that’s the bigger question: What’s the long term play with GTA 6?”.

    Industry observers note that the next few days will be flooded with GTA 6 content, clips, and brand activations. How that extends into the holidays and beyond into 2027, when Rockstar will release the game on PC and likely add its online component, remains to be seen.

    “There couldn’t be more momentum headed into this game launch…I’m a little concerned it is going to have a hard time living up to the hype,” said Duchscher.

    Recent findings suggest that eichen thinks creator creativity may keep the hype train going. “It’s almost impossible to guess what’s going to come out of this because people are so creative…[creators are] going to build fresh things that we never imagined,” he stated.

    Creators are tapping into their massive content libraries for syndication opportunities that pay dividends.

    #112508. Inside Nike’s initiative to turn creators into brand builders

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1482 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Inside Nike’s initiative to turn creators into brand builders

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Nike’s turnaround blueprint gives creators a bigger role in building the brand.
    • That became clear at its investor day earlier this week (November 17), where execs spent plenty of time on getting closer to athletes and stretched the definition of one to take in far more people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Nike’s turnaround blueprint gives creators a bigger role in building the brand.

    That became clear at its investor day earlier this week (November 17), where execs spent plenty of time on getting closer to athletes and stretched the definition of one to take in far more people.

    “When we say athlete, we mean athlete in the broadest sense possible. If you have a body, you are an athlete,” CEO Eliott Hill told investors.

    It has been revealed that that definition puts everyday participants alongside elite competitors. Separately, Nike is looking to bring creators, cultural voices and local communities closer to the brand as part of its growth strategy. Together, these moves are part of “Full Stride Ahead”, the strategy Nike is counting on to get back to sustainable, profitable growth. Doing so rests on three pillars the brand’s top brass call “Epic”, “Connected” and “Fast.”. They cover product innovation, consumer relationships and speed to market. Connected is where creates and athletes come in.

    According to recent reports, brand president Amy Montagne said Nike is changing how it spends its marketing dollars, with more weight on “grassroots connections, local creators and relevant cultural voices”. She said the goal is to reach communities through “the right people, in the right places and at the right moments”.

    Industry observers note that the splashy camopaigns and superstar deals will carry on. Next to them, Nike is building a looser network of local influence, informed by research across more than 10 markets where it quizzed athletes, retailers, creators and tastemakers about how tastes shift from place to place. Local teams will get more say over product creation, assortments and how the brand indicates up in each market. The shift is particularly clear in China, where Nike acknowledged that its previous model was too centralized toward its headquarters in Beaverton, Oregon. It is now moving towards more locally driven product creation and giving teams closer to shoppers greater influence over decisions.

    According to recent reports, that means changes for creators too. Nike wants their help reading an audience and translating product into local culture, a job that starts well before any campaign lives. The company looks to expand its use of creator networks, entertainment partnerships and athlete-led storytelling.

    “Putting the onus on the regions is the right way of thinking as long as it goes deep enough,” mentioned James Kirkham, founder of brand consultancy Iconic. “With JD Sports we worked on ‘second cities’ like Liverpool, Rotterdam and Lyon (these are often port cities for various historic cultural hot spot reasons), which tend to get to culture first.”.

    The trends in Liverpool are very different from those just 30 miles down the road in Manchester, he continued, right down to the shape and fit of some jogging bottoms and a brand that lumps the two together has already lost so knowing that sheer nuance and level of detail and flagging it is key to proper authentic hits.

    In a recent development, nike’s football plans show this is supposed to work. The company built the strategy around a consumer archetype it calls the “Mad Baller” — a football obsessed teenager who plays the game, watches it and dresses the part. Nike is chasing that kid across what it calls pitch, stands and street which ties elite players and performance boots to fan culture, fashion, creators and grassroots football.

    According to recent reports, some of that was on display over the summer. At the World Cup, its “Rip the Script” campaign got 5.7 billion content views, according to the investor day presentation. During it, execs also highlighted how a newly introduced generation of creators brought its sotires into football culture generating hundreds of millions of views. Nike then spread the story across individual athlete content, creator collabs, product drops, retail experiences and local tournaments.

    Sources indicate that sponsored athletes are in a line for a similar rethink. A player’s value to Nike used to rest mostly on performance and visibility during tournaments. Now, the organization wants their training, persona;lities and fan relationships to keep the brand in people’s feeds all year. That also opens up collaborations with creators that reach well beyond the athletes own sport.

    It has been revealed that nike seems more interested in bringing creators into how the brand gets built than in buying sponsored posts. A running creator may understand amateur runners better than an ad agency does. A local fashion figure in Lagos or Seoul may have a sharper sense of how sport feeds into streetwear in their city than a global marketing team in Beaverton. People like that can spot trends early, shape storytelling and turn passing interest into actual participation.

    According to recent reports, plenty of that work will still look like ordinary campaign and content distribution, of course, and most creators won’t become long-term strategic partners. Yet Nike’s growing use of creator networks could become a competitive advantage, particularly when creators have real standing in a sporting or cultural community. For these creators, the opportunity could extend beyond sponsored content into partnerships involving product, communities and intellectual property.

    Nike offered another example of this approach through its Studio Fleece launch. The initiative brought together more than 100 athletes, entertainers, creators and stylists, combining product seeding, creative participation and Nike By You experiences. The collection was distributed across more than 6,000 retail outlets. Nike described it as the largest new apparel launch in its history, with the highest proportion of sales made at full price of any fleece launch.

    None of this matters if it doesn’t contribute to sales so Nike is focusing on five priority sports: running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor plus sportswear. More often than not those efforts will be focused on 23 countries that Nike expects to deliver about 90% of its growth opportunity between fiscal 2028 and 2031. The goal is around $5 billion in extra revenue by fiscal 2031, compared with fiscal 2027. Nike expeccts about $4 billion of that to come from the five sports and about one billion to come from sportswear.

    Running was the proof point the investor day presentations kept coming back to. The category has delivered nine consecutive quarters of growth from the first quarter of its fiscal year in 2025 through to the first for 2027, including six straight quarters of double-digit growth. That’s around £1 billion revenue for the business.

    Nike’s Montagne described the wider goal as building “a repeatable engine to create demand,” and that’s the phrase investors are likely to hold the company to. Indeed, Nike wants a model it can roll out across sports and markets deliberately so it isn’t waiting for the occasional cultural moment to land.

    A bigger role in a brand’s strategy raises new questions for creators, athletes and the people who represent them. A creator who helps a brand understand a community and build demand there might reasonably look for something beyond a campaign fee. An athlete who helps build a content platform or a product line could push to share in the long-term value they help create. And as brand-run realtor networks get more sophisticated, ownership of the audience, the content and the IP becomes a bigger part of any negotiation.

    Investor Days are always about a manufacturer’s growth looks so no surprise that compensation models weren’t on the agenda. Those conversations are more likely to happen deal by deal, and in turn create another boon for the cottage industry of agencies, talent managers and creator businesses that have emerged around the creator economy to put together partnerships that account for the wider value creators and athletes bring.

    In a recent development, “If I were managing a creator right now then I’d tell them to play up everything specific about themselves: their expertise, their obsessions, their accent, their postcode. Get into the nerdiest detail you’ve got and bring every bit of it to life,” mentioned Iconic’s Kirkham “The deals Nike is describing will go to deep experts with a real local standing and a million views on last decade’s platforms won’t get anyone really bothered or doing the marketing for you any more, you need to go beautifully deep and nuanced.”.

    In Graphic Detail: Welcome to the agentic commerce quarter

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Holiday 2026 is shaping up as the first season where the shopping agent actually pays — solidifying Q4 as the agentic commerce quarter.
    • It has been revealed that openAI rolled out ChatGPT wallet this week to push agent purchase through retailer checkouts, alongside a commerce partner playbook aimed at helping businesses prepare for a future of more agent-led purchase.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Holiday 2026 is shaping up as the first season where the shopping agent actually pays — solidifying Q4 as the agentic commerce quarter.

    It has been revealed that openAI rolled out ChatGPT wallet this week to push agent purchase through retailer checkouts, alongside a commerce partner playbook aimed at helping businesses prepare for a future of more agent-led purchase. Google began rolling its UCP-powered checkout in Canada through AI Mode and Gemini. Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site. Walmart lets customers cap an agent’s spending at $50, $100 or $200. And Bain reckons roughly one in four online shoppers initiative to start their holiday shopping journeys on an AI platform.

    Put together, agentic commerce is having a growth spurt even if it’s still a while from growing up.

    Sources indicate that agentic commerce is moving from hypothetical to commercial opportunity, with platforms and retailers beginning to position themselves for a new way of shopping. U.S. retail e-commerce sales completed through end-to-end agentic commerce are forecast to reach $1.44 billion this year, according to eMarketer. That figure is expected to increase 10.6% to $1.59 billion in 2027, a further 11% increase to $1.76 billion in 2028 and reach $2.17 trillion by 2030.

    Marketers are already adapting their strategies to account for AI agents, although the focus so far seems to be making brands discoverable, rather than enabling agents to buy from them.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Gartner’s 2026 Marketing Strategy and Engagement Survey, 61% of senior marketing leaders have adapted content and SEO/AEO to improve machine interpretability. A further 42% are monitoring and correcting misinformation about their brands in AI-generated outputs, while 39% have tailored product information, pricing or offers for machine and agent decision-making.

    But the same survey found that fewer have taken proper steps yet to accommodate agent-led transactions. Around a third (30%) of marketers have designed interfaces or workflows for agent transactions, while 32% manage machines and agents as a distinct audience alongside human customers.

    Brands might be getting ready for agents, but most consumers aren’t yet comfortable letting one spend their money unsupervised.

    Sources indicate that according to U.S. identity and access management company Okta’s Customer Identity Trends Report 2026, when consumers were asked how likely they’d be to let an AI agent complete a purchase without reviewing it first, only a third (31%) said they were very or rather likely to. At the same time, 67% of those surveyed said they were unlikely to let an AI agent finish a purchase without review, while 41% said they wouldn’t at all.

    Of course, there are exceptions. Early adopters of the tech are far more trusting. Nearly two thirds (62%) stated they’d let an AI agent complete a purchase without checking, and 42% said they’d be very likely to.

    The gap suggests the hard part of agentic commerce may not be getting the right tech, but instead building the right amount of trust.

    Shoppers might not be handing over full control to the checkout just yet, but AI tools are already influencing where they go to buy, and the visitors those tools send are more likely to spend.

    Industry observers note that in September, shoppers who arrived at U.S. retail e-commerce sites from AI tools converted 90% better than those from other channels, according to Adobe Digital Insights. That’s the highest level Adobe has recorded, and a sharp turnaround from August 2025 when AI traffic converted 9% worse than other channels.

    For major e-commerce businesses, agentic commerce could have implications beyond how products are sold. It could also change how retailers make money from helping shoppers to discover them.

    Amazon, for example, generated $68.5 billion in net sales from its online stores during Q3 2026, alongside $46.5 billion from third-party seller services, and $20 billion from ad services, according to Enders Analysis.

    As agentic commerce becomes a more natural part of the consumer journey, shoppers may increasingly rely on agents to identify and recommend products rather than browse sponsored listings. It could affect Amazon’s business in different ways: its fulfilment infrastructure could support transactions initiated elsewhere, while its advertising business could face pressure if fewer shoppers encounter paid placements on its platform.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This story was first published by Digiday sibling Modern Retail.

    Energy drink brand Celsius is rapidly expanding its footprint across the sports landscape.

    The manufacturer is increasingly leveraging partnerships with major sports leagues, college athletics and high-profile athletic events to connect with health-conscious consumers. In 2026 alone, Celsius has announced several sponsorships and marketing activations across professional and amateur sporting events.

    According to recent reports, in August, Celsius also became the official energy drink sponsor of ESPN’s College GameDay. The multi-year partnership kicked off for the 2026 season at major campus stops, with activations including run clubs and tailgates. For its college football NIL (name, image and likeness) integration, Celsius partnered with college football analyst Kirk Herbstreit, alongside a collegiate roster that included Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood and Oregon quarterback Dante Moore. To close out the year, Celsius is delving deeper into the burgeoning world of Formula 1. The energy drink brand signed British professional driver Jessica Hawkins ahead of the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix this month. By aligning its brand with active lifestyles and high-performance athletics, Celsius aims to solidify its position as a better-for-you functional beverage for elite competitors and everyday fitness enthusiasts.

    Many professional sporting events are sponsored by major hydration or alcohol brands. However, Celsius states its origins as a better-for-you alternative to sugary energy drinks position it as a product that can support fitness enthusiasts and athletes.

    In a recent development, running has also rapidly become a focus of Celsius’ sports marketing strategy. Most recently, the brand returned with a Club Celsius pop-up at the Fresh York City Marathon, which included a multi-day takeover in Brooklyn along the race route. Throughout the fall, the brand also sponsored Diplo’s Run Club stops in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. In a related category, fitness events and competitions are a growing marketing opportunity for Celsius. Earlier this year, the brand also became the official global energy drink partner of the fitness competition ATHX Games.

    Kyle Watson, CMO of Celsius, told Modern Retail that with the ongoing Live. Fit. Go. campaign at the center of the brand, sports is a natural and effective space for Celsius to show up. The 360 campaign, which targets active consumers, introduced in 2025 with TV, paid ads, organic social, out-of-home and experiential activations.

    According to recent reports, “What differentiates us is the breadth of our presence,” Watson noted. “Celsius isn’t defined by a single sport; we’re building meaningful connections across the entire sports landscape.”.

    That has meant heavy investment across collegiate sports for the past few years, largely through strategic NIL partnerships with athletes across football, basketball and gymnastics. “This year, we took that presence to the next level through our multi-year partnership with ESPN’s College GameDay,” noted Watson. Through Celsius Combine, a football-inspired fan event, along with campus run clubs, Watson said the brand is offering immersive experiences that embody the Live. Fit. Go. campaign.

    According to recent reports, more and more, brands are using sporting events to do official or proximity marketing to capture fan excitement. This has become a popular tactic during big events like the Super Bowl and even college sports tournaments.

    Anjali Bal, associate professor of marketing at Babson College, said today’s consumers are highly invested in sporting events, which makes them prime moments for marketing campaigns.

    “Adrenaline and psychological responses are high” at these events, Bal stated. “When you tie this to team loyalty and the desire to belong, consumers are more open to messaging and brands; they align with their values and their teams.”.

    In a recent development, that remarked, Watson said Celsius views its sports strategy as extending beyond traditional sporting events. For example, Watson said, “Through our multi-year partnership with Aston Martin Aramco, one of the most ambitious teams in Formula 1, we’re showing up at key races and connecting with a premium, global audience.” Watson added that Celsius’ Formula 1 presence is another example of how the brand is trying to credibly align with elite athletes and competitors across various disciplines. “Because our product is a drink for athletes, regardless of the sport,” Watson added.

    Sources indicate that looking ahead, Watson said Celsius will continue to evolve its sports strategy to reach people more often and in more meaningful ways. “In 2027, consumers can expect even more impactful partnerships with leading teams, elite athletes and high-performance programs, all designed to bring the Live. Fit. Go. mentality to life,” Watson said.

    Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • Mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and new media.
    • Industry observers note that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Mail Metro Media now thinks “more like a talent agency” and commissions “like a broadcaster”, according to Hannah Blake, its managing director of creator and new media. Its creators have, in other words, become the business.

    Industry observers note that audiences tune in for them, brands pay to reach those audiences, and the deals have grown from around £5,000 apiece to worth seven figures in October. Holding on to those creators is now as key as finding them since any one who leaves for an outside agent can take the audience and advertisers along too.

    Blake spelled out that risk on stage at the Digiday Media Strategies London event in October.

    “The huge risk is that we make these people super famous and then they go and get signed by a different agent,” she stated.

    So in September the ad sales arm for the Daily Mail hired David White from Whalar as head of creators, with a brief to build an in-house talent agency that represents its creators and signs outside talent too. White was the first hire for the firm’s Stars business in Newly introduced York, the talent management arm that handles creators’ careers beyond brand deals and was also a senior talent manager there.

    Recent findings suggest that what the business ultimately ends up with is still open. Blake described something that “potentially could look more like a talent agency and an employer,” and she hopes to have it in market by the end of the year. The final shape matters because running a talent agency would be a big change of job for a newspaper group’s ad sales team. It exists to sell audiences to brands while an agent’s job is to get the best deal for the talent. Mail Metro Media would be trying to do both at once.

    That’s the potted history of how Mail Metro Media reached this point. The full story is a lot more nuanced.

    It started four years ago when Daily Mail released Eliza, a social-only brand for young women fronted by six fashion and beauty creators. Its hit format, “Guess Which Outfit’s Most Expensive”, puts two women on the street, one in a £10,000 outfit and the other in a high-street copy, and leaves viewers to guess which is which. It kept going viral, people kept coming back and advertisers soon followed. That’s despite it being relatively small next to the rest of the Mail’s portfolio, and yet “we were doing lots of direct advertisers relationships quite promptly”, Blake remarked. Fast forward to now,  and brands often book content on Eliza and then want its creators posting on their own accounts too, which Mail Metro Media packages into the deal.

    It has been revealed that the Mail’s own TikTok was a different story. The Mail and Metro introduced on the platform around the same time as Eliza and the former became the biggest news publisher there, with 20 million followers, on the back of rapid-fire news clips. But the money didn’t follow. “The huge issue was there was no monetization there,” Blake noted, even though publishers had widely expected TikTok to start paying them for views. Advertisers weren’t keen either, Every rival was posting the same kind of clips and the Daily Mail couldn’t build a brand into footage it had brought in from elsewhere.

    In a recent development, together, they demonstrated the publisher that the money was in demonstrates it owned and creators audiences came back for. It shifted course accordingly, and over the past year it relaunched the Mail and Metro on social around repeatable shows it owns, such as the sports debate show “Dugout Debate” with creators at the front and helping shape them. Blake noted the operation now pulls 5 billion monthly video views across 10 brands and signed its first seven-figure deal last month. With that success comes a latest kind of risk. The creators fronting those shows have built followings of their own and “now some of the superstars are beginning to emerge,” Blake said. Left unchecked, the publisher ends up making stars for outside agencies to sign.

    In a recent development, in some ways, the publisher has already been acting like an agent of sorts. Alongside its core bundle where brands pay one flat rate for a run of content with “no differentiation between the talent,” Blake remarked it has spent the past year selling individual creators on their own channels. It calls this add-on “Creator Amp.” One example is Mimi Yates, a young journalist who fronts much of the news output and has built a following of her own. Brands can book her as part of a wider campaign or on her own, and on their personal accounts the creators “all set their own rates,” Blake said.

    That arrangement was easy to manage while the talent was still unknown.

    It has been revealed that “When we started, our creators were all emerging,” Blake said. With bigger names now coming through, the publisher wants something sturdier. “We are now at the point where we’re beginning to formalize that relationship a bit more,” she said, and hiring White was the first step.

    It has been revealed that he will recruit from two places. One is from its own staff. The other is outside talent Blake described as “the next generation of emerging news and entertainment talent”.

    Moves like this bring some awkward conversations with them. Daily Mail’s creators are salaried and Nathan Aspell, director of the Fresh Media division, said the manufacturer owns the IP they develop. Blake described those same creators setting their own rates on their own channels. How the money is split between the employer and agent will go a long way to deciding whether a breakout star sticks around.

    Axel Springer’s version hands journalists a share of the financial results in return for production, marketing and distribution. Daily Mail hasn’t noted what its agency will charge.

    Then there’s the small matter of journalism. The same person can read the headlines and sell the mascara, and the publisher would be both their employer and their agent. That’s a lot of hats for one newsroom.

    According to recent reports, white’s first signings will show how far the publisher intends to take this venture. Blake thinks publishers are headed this way regardless. “I actually think it’s just a byproduct of where the opportunity is,” she mentioned.

    It has been revealed that for a lot of publishers, signing talent still feels like someone else’s business and talk of newsrooms turning into agencies tends to raise eyebrows. Blake sees it as following the money, which increasingly sits with “people-centric IP that exists across multiple different touchpoints”.

    Sources indicate that plenty of rivals are following it too. Axel Springer rolled out its own spin on the same idea last month, while Hearst did so earlier this week. Increasingly, publishers see a talent operation as the next step in their latest pivot to video, which runs on personalities whose audiences, and the ad money chasing them, follow them wherever they go.

    “Publishers are responding to the audience’s desire for personality-led formats while limiting strategic dependence on individual journalists and managing talent,” said Laura Darcey, research analyst at Enders Analysis.

    It has been revealed that editor’s note: An earlier version of this article remarked David White ran Whalar’s Stars business in Fresh York. He was the first hire for the division in New York.

    Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    He’s equally comfortable at the negotiating table or on skates in an ice rink.

    He doesn’t do it himself but he knows principal media is part of the business.

    He’s mentioned to have once humbled the CEO of a major cable network group by holding back $200 million of his clients’ media spend when that CEO tried to bully him into massive price increases.

    He’s the longest-serving head of investment in media. And now, John Muszynski, legendary media investment executive with Publicis Media, plans to retire.

    After 45 years at one holding firm and negotiating nearly as many upfronts over that span, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he aims to continue to consult with the holdco.

    In a recent development, chicago-based Muszynski, who oversees decision-making on what Publicis estimates to be 40% of the U.S. video marketplace inventory, is arguably the last of the old-school heads of investment that have seen the upfronts morph into the byzantine bazaar it is today.

    In a recent development, “For nearly five decades, I’ve had a front row seat to the industry’s transformation,” Muszynski told Digiday. “It’s gone from three networks to always-on content spanning the entire digital ecosystem. It’s been fascinating to be a part of it all.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the avid ice hockey fan, hunter and fisherman (when he’s not negotiating) got his start in 1981 as a planner for Leo Burnett’s burgeoning media unit, handling longtime Publicis clients including Kimberly-Clark, McDonald’s and Kellogg’s. That unit eventually became standalone media agency Starcom, for which he rose to CEO of Starcom USA from 2005-2009. He then helped to build Spark Foundry from a 65-person boutique into a 3,000-person media agency.

    Industry observers note that in 2016, Publicis formed Publicis Media Exchange, which harnessed the collective buying clout of what was then Starcom, Mediavest, Spark, Zenith, Optimedia and Blue 449 media agencies. He was the lead negotiator when that formed, and became chairman of the group in 2022.

    The execs who sat across from him at the negotiating table said they always felt they got a fair shake — in part because Muszynski always came prepared, was knowledgable and true to his word.

    According to recent reports, “John has been a tremendous influence on generations of marketers, agency team members and publishers,” said Mark Marshall, chairman of global advertising and partnerships at NBCUniversal. “He has always put his clients’ objectives at the forefront and pushed all of us to deliver for those clients. He is the epitome of ‘a handshake is his word’.”.

    According to recent reports, rita Ferro, president, global advertising, disney, was even more personal in her assessment of working with Muszynski. “John is a legend in this business and from the moment we met, he became a trusted partner and more importantly a dear friend,” she said.

    Sean Moran, COO at Evergreen Trading agency, who negotiated with Muszynski during his 24 years as an ad sales exec with Viacom until 2020, thinks of Muszynski as a contemporary of the old-school buyers of the TV business, from Grey Advertising’s Jon Mandel to UM’s Donna Wolfe, and from Omnicom’s John Swift to GroupM’s Rino Scanzoni.

    Industry observers note that “When I was running MTV and we had a major upfront event, and had to get people there, if I could get John Muszynski to fly in and come to my event, that was a huge win,” stated Moran. ”He represented so much gravitas. Obviously he controlled a lot of budgets, but it was also because he was so smart and yet had such empathy for good people. You couldn’t bullshit him. He was a good Midwestern guy who could talk about a great deal over over a steak, but he did his homework and knew his numbers.”.

    Industry observers note that moran said Muszynski often set the marketplace as “the main controller” of the upfronts. “One of his negotiating tactics was, ‘Yeah, I haven’t seen everything, but boy, it looks down’,” said Moran. “If he respected your inventory, you could do a deal with him fairly rapidly and cut through the chaff. He was known to pull that with one or two people that were at the front of the line, and protect his clients. He would therefore set the marketplace for himself. It was very smart.”.

    Industry observers note that although Muszynski will retire from his full-time position at PMX, he will stay on to consult through 2027, working with Joel Lunenfeld who leads PMX globally and Mark Griffin, who oversees all investment in the U.S. as chief investment officer.

    #112485. Industry News: Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (676 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Correcting the TV ad market’s imperfect shift to streaming

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.
    • The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Evan Rutchik, president and Chief Strategy Officer, Viamedia.ai.

    The TV ad industry’s shift from linear to streaming is real, but the financial truth underlying that shift may not align with many people’s perception of the transition. That’s because the movement of ad budgets from linear to streaming has hardly been evenly paced.

    Streaming’s share of ad revenue is indeed growing at major media companies, including The Walt Disney Tech giant, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. But their earnings tell a different story: Linear revenue is falling faster than streaming revenue is rising. The shift is happening, but it’s not benefiting content owners as expected.

    In a recent development, the core problem is a supply-demand imbalance. Streaming ad revenue is growing through increased volume, not higher prices. Upcoming inventory floods in, making cheap inventory abundant. As major subscription services continue to promote free ad-supported streaming tiers, the buyers’ market will only continue.

    The solution is to grow demand, not increase prices. Fortunately, the ad dollars needed to support the streaming market already exist, sitting in local and midmarket budgets that haven’t been able to buy national CTV efficiently. The opportunity is to bring these advertisers into the broader video and streaming market, then develop ways to keep them investing.

    Correcting the imbalance requires creating new demand, then ensuring that content quality and product performance are strong enough to eventually shift pricing dynamics.

    When it comes to growth, the glut of cheap national SVOD supply may be a problem for programmers, but it’s an opportunity for local and midmarket advertisers. If the current streaming market is largely aimed at Fortune 500 companies, the industry has to consider the thousands of smaller advertisers that make steady annual investments in local linear buys. Taken collectively, these advertisers represent billions of dollars in ad budgets.

    Because these advertisers have smaller budgets, many haven’t tried streaming. It is more cost-efficient for them to execute local and spot buys on linear than to invest in targeted or national streaming campaigns. These advertisers are still seeing real success reaching millions of linear viewers, so they understand the power of TV. They just need an entry point for CTV. Solving this glitch would allow demand to flow steadily into the market.

    Once that demand enters the market, additional steps must happen. CPMs fall when inventory is sold as undifferentiated tonnage. With platforms like Disney+ and Netflix exploring free ad-supported tiers, even more low-cost supply will enter the market. But cheap supply that doesn’t perform isn’t worth an advertiser’s investment. If that inventory doesn’t deliver results for advertisers outside the Fortune 500, those advertisers will invest their budgets elsewhere, creating another demand imbalance.

    The answer lies in household addressability. While this is available on some streaming platforms, it’s still largely absent from the overall TV market, including linear. Household-level addressability turns cheap impressions into targeted impressions worth buying, even within highly premium inventory. The more information brands have about who will see their ads and whether those ads are likely to resonate with the viewer, the more they are likely to pay.

    It is no secret that streaming is the future of TV, and shifting revenue numbers reflect that. To build a sustainable future for media companies and advertisers, the entire ecosystem must first provide ease of access and then addressability.

    Making streaming easier to buy at scale would help solve the demand problem. Once more advertisers are in the market, addressability creates greater competition for impressions, solving the pricing imbalance.

    This future is out there, provided the industry takes a few steps in the right direction.

    Partner insights from Viamedia.ai.

    OpenAI rewrites ChatGPT Business Hub terms after legal language raises concerns

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • OpenAI has revised the terms for its fresh ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch.
    • Launched last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    OpenAI has revised the terms for its fresh ChatGPT Business Hub days after its launch. The change came after Digiday reported that lawyers viewed the original language as potentially limiting businesses’ ability to bring certain legal claims against the company.

    Launched last week, the Business Hub gives businesses that verify their accounts direct data on how their websites appear in ChatGPT, including mentions, profile views, clicks and discovery topics. For publishers, it’s a first-party view of activity they’ve largely had to estimate.

    Before the revision, Section 10 of OpenAI’s terms of service for businesses using ChatGPT appeared to require those businesses to give up certain legal claims against OpenAI, lawyers told Digiday. They said the language could apply to claims involving content published on their websites, before they signed up.

    Alan Chapell, privacy expert and founder of Chapell and Associates, mentioned publishers who signed up for ChatGPT’s Business Hub and accepted the terms could have faced restrictions on how they pursued such claims against OpenAI.

    Recent findings suggest that the terms included a mandatory arbitration provision and class-action waiver, potentially requiring businesses to resolve disputes individually and outside of court, Chapell said. The provision was broadly worded to cover certain claims that arose before the agreement was accepted, he explained.

    Businesses had 30 days to opt out of arbitration, but if they did not, they could have faced limits on their ability to obtain evidence, pursue appeals and establish legal precedent through public court proceedings, Chapell added.

    In a recent development, hours after Digiday first contacted OpenAI on Nov. 18, the terms were revised. They now include a waiver of businesses’ rights to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data, according to an IP and tech lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

    “There are still some restrictions here but they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse. A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages,” they said.

    When approached for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the previous version of the terms “were not intended to cover this scenario,” and confirmed it updated the terms on Nov. 18.

    It has been revealed that “We continually evaluate the language in our Terms to make sure they are as clear as possible,” the spokesperson added in a statement. “The updated terms replace the separate ‘covered claims’ provision with language in Section 5.2 that ties the release to claims arising from a business’s Business Agent, including the use of customer data with that agent.”.

    Sources indicate that one industry exec, who requested anonymity, told Digiday they advised publishers’ legal teams to be cautious around some of the potential implications of OpenAI’s terms for businesses, after they were originally published on Nov. 10.

    Although the terms have been revised, several lawyers who spoke to Digiday said the original version was likely deliberate.

    “This is certainly not an oversight because they put these terms out there,” said Gary Kibel, partner at law firm Davis+ Gilbert, which advises media and advertising clients. “It was incredibly intentional, and they were seeking to use this opportunity to get a release and wavier for any of these claims. It seems to be quite aggressive to do that.”.

    Kibel said the revised terms still require businesses to waive certain legal claims related to their use of ChatGPT Business Hub and its AI Business Agents (essentially a business-specific chatbot), but no longer extend that waiver to unrelated legal disputes with OpenAI.

    It has been revealed that openAI’s changes come just weeks after Meta faced major backlash from publishers over its new commercial terms, which would have allowed the firm to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users. The proposed changes spurred a global, coordinated pushback from publishers, trade bodies, and government officials and regulators. In response, Meta revealed it would pause the rollout until it has had time to explain the changes to key stakeholders and partners.

    In a recent development, openAI’s terms revision also follows tensions between publishers and AI companies over the use of published content. Documents unsealed in The New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft two months ago revealed tech giants were treating published content as free fuel for AI products that threatened their very existence.

    Whatever prompted the revision, it may do little to ease publishers’ broader concerns about how AI companies use their content, and the terms attached to new tools built around that content.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

    ChatGPT’s fresh AI visibility and click data can help inform publishers’ GEO strategies and complement third-party analytics.

    Creators are tapping into their massive content libraries for syndication opportunities that pay dividends.

    Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • According to recent reports, this article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics.
    • Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    According to recent reports, this article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most notable information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →.

    Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

    “You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” said Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

    As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

    The number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

    The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

    In a recent development, currently, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

    The days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

    According to recent reports, “For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” remarked Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”.

    Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

    While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

    In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

    “What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” noted Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

    Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

    Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media owners to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

    “They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” said Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

    The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

    Although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

    It has been revealed that but as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” noted Wedderburn.

    Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

    “The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” said Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

    There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

    A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

    “We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” said Wedderburn.

    In a recent development, that’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

    “If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to strategy creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”.

    Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.
